It seemed as if we didn't get to understand their relationship enough, or the time it was shown, not much happened except for a banality of events. I had no emotional attachment to any single character in this film. The only time I did was in the first 10-20 minutes or so, where the two protagonists mention their affection for each other in a specific manner, which is somewhat relevant to me, but this alone doesn't do much for the film in terms of what it should do In honesty, the only voices that I heard in the forest (my bed, from which I was lying viewing this) were, "Not again, Netflix has once again masqueraded another romance drama in fancy colour palettes and heart-warming cinematography." This film truly disappointed me. Such is life -just like Roberts answer to his predicament, I had lost two hours of my life that I could've spent elsewhere: writing reviews that will never influence anyone but my subconsciousness. It was such a strong beginning to lead to, basically nothing. The film has some charm. I like the normal life story of a regular man working in a labor intensive job to try and have a happy life with his wife and kid. He goes through hardship as year after year time slips by, losing more time with the people he loves. This is all great stuff and has me very invested, until it doesn’t. The film feels like it loses direction. Some things that bothered Robert early in the film have no meaning later on. At least there was a conflict that gave the film some plot. After the big fire that leaves him in grief, he does almost nothing the rest of the film. There is a good scene or two though, especially the crying scenes that Joel Edgerton nails, but it doesn’t move his character along almost at all. It’s just deep conversation after deep conversation until we get to the final 20 minutes of the film (which is completely rushed/unearned and the worst part of the whole story). I never minded the slow pace of the film because I was expecting it to go somewhere, but it didn’t. Two big positives: The cinematography is so interesting. Whether the focus of the shot is down the middle or in the corner of the screen, it’s always intriguing. 1000% makes the film better. The acting is very moving at times. Joel Edgerton and William Macy both have emotional performances that enhance their characters greatly.

Vale la pena, di tanto in tanto, diminuire il battito, accorgersi di ciò che c’è intorno a noi e unirci a tutto. Un po’ come succede a Robert Grainier nel finale del film Train Dreams. In un periodo storico nel quale si tende a velocizzare l’arte e diminuire i tempi di fruibilità per mancanza di attenzione, bisogna saper tornare alle origini e riconciliarsi. Saper ascoltare davvero il mondo e le emozioni che ci travolgono, belle o brutte che esse siano, è in qualche modo necessario. È una parte di messaggio implicita che può essere estrapolata dalla pellicola del 2025 di Clint Bentley. Se vi aspettate concentrati di modernità, allora non è qualcosa adatto a voi, ma riesce a esprimere ugualmente concetti attuali pur essendo contestualizzati nel passato. Ci sono sensazioni e delicatezze che non contemplano i ritmi attuali e hanno bisogno di essere espresse nella loro forma autentica. Dilatare, per assaporare a pieno un’esperienza diversa, che magari non vi verrà in mente di riguardare, ma in qualche modo lascia il segno. Ciò che colpisce fortemente è la componente fotografica, un lavoro che rende molto bene l’idea del regista. Ma gli elementi che impressionano maggiormente sono i suoni, i rumori di qualunque cosa. Che sia la caduta di un albero secolare tagliato, oppure l’esplosione di un carico di dinamite, ogni dettaglio rappresenta la sottolineatura del regista all’ascolto. Come se davvero fossero queste le vere sensazioni di vita. A farcelo notare, in alcuni frangenti, è lo stesso protagonista. Quando chiede, nei momenti di intimità, alla sua compagna Claire Thompson di pronunciare il suo nome, perché è solo quando è lei a pronunciarlo che gli piace così tanto. E poi c’è il tema forte del dramma e degli anni che passano. I tormenti con cui dover convivere, la tragedia della perdita delle persone amate, come per Robert in quell’incidente fatale, sono persecuzioni dell’anima. Così come lo specchio del periodo storico e le piaghe del razzismo e delle differenze etniche che lo sfiorano. Sono tutti macigni che il personaggio principale si porta addosso più dei suoi vestiti. Tra incubi notturni e le chiacchiere di vecchi boscaioli incontrati nelle stagioni lavorative. La clessidra della vita continua a scorrere inesorabile, spesso senza rendere conto di attimi che ormai sono passati. La chiusura finale è quasi un tentativo di spronare a vivere emozioni forti, di percepire in profondità per non restare soltanto sul pelo dell’acqua. Momenti intensi che riescono a mostrarti la realtà e forse, finalmente, far capire il senso di tutto.

A beautiful movie as far as cinematography is concerned, but that is, unfortunately, about all that can be said for it. Much of the movie is unnecessarily narrated in a way that insults the intelligence of attentive viewers. The story completely falls flat, particularly the main character’s unaccountable arc of crushing guilt, which he experiences for many reasons but no good ones (e.g. for a crime that he did not commit, but rather actively tried to prevent, and maybe also for cutting down trees). His guilt is also just there as a floating plot point that ultimately doesn’t affect any of his actions. The woke racial and environmental messaging was somehow extremely heavy-handed and impossibly convoluted at the same time; I wouldn’t know what to take away from the movie even if I agreed with its creators. The characters were generally uninteresting, and the ending was somehow bad enough to be disappointing even considering how bad the rest of the story was. At the end of the day, Train Dreams is a beautiful movie in terms of visuals, but would be better as a screen-saver than a movie.

This movie was very disappointing. It had beautiful visuals and a good soundtrack, but everything else fell flat. It gave the impression of a director much less intelligent than Terrance Malik trying to mimic his style. The narrator is extremely overly didactic, almost like he’s speaking so audience members scrolling on their phones can still understand what’s happening. Though it spans decades, and the change in the times is meant to be a central theme, it really doesn’t do a great job of communicating those changes visually. There is some woke stuff in general such as a reference to mass deportations in the first three minutes and a goofy anti-logging environmental message. Most baffling is the main character’s recurring guilt dream. Early on in the movie, he witnesses a (hamfistedly portrayed) racially motivated murder of a Chinese railway worker. Throughout the movie he has dreams of that man, and seems to feel guilt about the incident. However, he did not participate in the murder, nor did he even stand idly by. He acted in the indisputably objectively correct manner and attempted to stop the murder even to the point of attempting to physically stop the men preparing to commit it. His guilt over something he witnessed but actively tried to stop is ridiculous.

A camera glides through a tunnel. A locomotive gathers speed as it crosses a timber bridge, hurtling toward the camera as if to crush the cinematic apparatus—and so the audience—beneath its wheels. Ash, steam, fenders and embers flare between the trees as an apocalyptic iron horse rides through the darkness. These are the evocations of an old world in which phantom-ride films, ghostly fairground thrills, and engines on ever-extending railways networks promised people a brighter, faster future. These are the machines that have shaped our present. But in telling us stories about the technological past, Train Dreams refuses to sell us an inhuman dream of modernity. People are framed amid grasses, ferns and trees. Sunlight dapples the forest floor through the leaves. Characters are submerged in water. The camera immerses us in the world as it was before aerial shots transformed how people saw the land. It’s a beautifully textured world that makes the weave of fabric and grain of wood feel as though it might be grazing your fingertips. The sympathetically crafted score entices us to follow Robert on his journey, even into the darkest realms. Those dark realms are singed by the baking heat of deadly forest fires and shaped by the relentlessness of human-caused environmental devastation. But while the film is gently critical of our complicity in destroying the trees that Robert cuts down, it is also caught up in the same, ongoing wrecking of nature. For the trees that appear on screen are in actuality cut, already dying trees that have been transported to a studio and used to dress a set. Train Dreams, then, is yet another contributor to the ecological nightmare that is the film industry.

Questo è quello che succede quando si cerca di imitare Terrence Malick e invece si finisce a fare un esercizio di stile, bello da vedere e freddo da morire. Train Dreams, ispirato all'omonimo romanzo, racconta la monotona vita di Robert Grainier (Joel Edgerton), un falegname che ama sua figlia e sua moglie più di qualsiasi altra cosa. Purtroppo, il lavoro lo tiene impegnato per molto tempo, rendendo pochi i momenti che può trascorrere con la sua famiglia, fino a quando un giorno non si ritroverà a fare i conti con un evento che gli cambierà la vita. Quando dico che vuole cercare di imitare un gigante del cinema come Malick, intendo che, così come lui, il regista Clint Bentley ha cercato di realizzare un'opera dove la fotografia vale da sola il biglietto e un film molto riflessivo che vive di sottrazione. In quest'ultimo elemento, però, ci troviamo davanti a un fallimento totale. Il film effettivamente cerca di trasformare una vita semplice e banale in una sorta di dramma riflessivo, cercando di dare almeno un senso di riflessione ed epicità dove apparentemente c'è il vuoto. C'è la routine. Purtroppo, il film non riesce in questo intento. Sono veramente pochi i momenti che colpiscono o riescono a suscitare un minimo di emozione o riflessione; per il resto, ci si trova davanti al piattume più totale. Le uniche note positive del film sono la fotografia, curata da Adolpho Veloso, che è splendida, e l'interpretazione di Joel Edgerton che, seppur, ripeto, non mi abbia causato nessuna emozione a livello facciale ed espressivo, non mi sento di bocciare. In conclusione, Train Dreams è un film che guarda ai giganti del passato cercando di imitarli, ma l'unica cosa che è riuscito a restituirmi è una sensazione di freddezza, perfino in un'opera che mostra l'esatto contrario.

Voto: 6.1/10 Interpretato da un solido Joel Edgerton, Train Dreams si muove tra i vasti e silenti spazi dell'America dei primi del Novecento, tentando di costruire un affresco elegiaco sulla vita di un taglialegna tra marginalità e progresso industriale. La confezione formale possiede indubbi meriti visivi, affidandosi a una fotografia di grande impatto che cattura la severità della natura selvaggia e a una recitazione misurata, capace di conferire una certa dignità materica ai momenti di solitudine del protagonista. Tuttavia, l'impianto complessivo finisce per adagiarsi su una lentezza eccessiva che spesso confonde la contemplazione con la stasi, penalizzato da una sceneggiatura frammentaria che fatica a dare coesione emotiva e drammaturgica agli snodi esistenziali raccontati, lasciando affiorare un senso di ripetitività e di progressivo distacco nello spettatore. L'opera ambisce a riflettere sul conflitto originario tra l'espansione della modernità capitalista e la dissoluzione delle comunità rurali, incarnando nel percorso del protagonista la condizione dell'individuo schiacciato dalle grandi trasformazioni storiche e tecnologiche. La figura del lavoratore isolato vorrebbe farsi archetipo della solitudine umana di fronte all'avanzare inesorabile di un'industrializzazione divoratrice, simboleggiata dall'arrivo delle ferrovie e del disboscamento intensivo. Eppure, il discorso ideologico e concettuale rimane spesso in superficie, imbrigliato in una retorica bucolica un po' scontata che guarda alla natura con un lirismo privo della forza corrosiva o della reale profondità critica necessarie a graffiare veramente lo spettatore. In conclusione, pur sorretto da una dignità artigianale innegabile e da un rigore formale apprezzabile, il film si arena in una narrazione a tratti evanescente e inconcludente, incapace di lasciare un segno duraturo e risolvendosi in un esercizio di stile nostalgico che rischia di scivolare troppo rapidamente nell'indifferenza.

cinematography is nice in a less iconographic way and moreso in a —as someone else put it— “instagram-edit-oriented-approach” with consistently saturated and contrasting nature shots of trees against sunsets, blue skies, red fires, etc. it certainly looks really good and exudes a genuinely calming energy, especially early on into the film. a nice, quiet picture of the life of a man who is caught in the midst of the rapidly changing 20th century, still grappling with loss and meaning in life. really anchors you into his life as it feels it churns to a stop while things grind on around him. i really do respect the message, but i find how the narrator takes such a large and active role in delivering it a little annoying. (1) he has a nasally, modern voice that stands out more against the earthy, serious energy of much of the rest of the movie and (2) he articulates almost every morale and meaning at pivotal scenes, never comfortable enough to let the image and acting speak for itself. telling me explicitly how grainier is feeling at all moments and narrating every wise-cliche-on-how-to-navigate-life was kind of annoying. finding out this was adapted from a book really made sense since it seems like the movie really didn’t want to let go of the mystical prose, so they layered it all over this movie. for a film that looks quite good, and is working with prose that has a unique brevity even i love, it just gets to feeling less poetical and more frictionless, mechanical, and cold. a friend who stopped by described it as a ‘documentary’, and though it may have been a look into grainier’s life on purpose, i certainly hope the movie didn’t intend to feel as as sanitized and impersonal as that. also the experience watching this was a little bit diluted so maybe if i revisit i can award the 4 ⭐️

The dead tree is as important as the living one. There is a stillness in the mere observing and absorbing of feelings, thoughts, people and places around Grainier, and how he makes sense of it. The film even looks like a dream or someone’s memory, a meditative kind of state, of going through it all, taking in every bit of impression. Time feels different, when a moment lingers for years, and years just pass in a moment. It binds together brutal reality with the yearning, which is poetic but mundane at the same time. It’s blunt about the relentless progress and how it ignores so much, leaving it all behind in the pursuit of that dream. The film simply shows how things change so gradually for one to simply sit around and ponder over it and look for what was missed and what really was achieved; was there a sameness one always thought would remain, and how suddenly does one realise that change only when it shows parts of it way too clearly visible. It's then also about what stays back, within, something that seems difficult to let go and see it change with everyone and everything around. What then does one look at, to keep going, with what’s left behind, and yet remains? There is a monotony in all of what happens, all that’s been held, and all that’s hurt, which is impermanent, and stays only as a memory. And it is in this ordinary being that there is a meaning that is often unseen in the grandness of life, but in moments that one remembers long after it passes. There, then nothing is pretentious. Mundane but real. Emotions are fleeting like nature, for they function to make you feel and see a thing, different at times. The idea remains; the emotions fluctuate in ways that evolve naturally and change in ways. The idea of something or someone stays sometimes. Some leave much quicker. Looking for something misplaced long ago, holding on to something for long, is all that’s beautifully connected and making one more and more human to all that one ever cared for. It is with this mundane nature that grief and yearning shape themselves, as the film doesn’t give an answer for what to do with it, but to live. As life goes on, forward, and sometimes backwards. In that, there are moments of small yet profound beauty. All else is forgotten, but to hold on to such a moment is to live while one is around. There’s then a beauty within the bitterness. One that lives along with surprising clarity till we choose to live with it.

Red Dead Melancholy. A quiet film about life. "The world's an old place. Probably nothing it hasn't seen by now." There is perhaps no better way to depict the ruthless passage of time than to capture the mundaneity of everyday life. Train Dreams does precisely that, presenting us with the life story of one Robert Grainier - a logger residing in America's Pacific Northwest. On the one hand, Robert's life could be dismissed as quite unremarkable, but that's where Train Dreams comes in - alluding to the fleeting joys, lingering heartaches, and bittersweet memories that make up life. It's a film that likes to emphasise how small we all are, and how trivial and fleeing life is within the grander scheme - but that that triviality is no good or bad thing... it just is. Life just is. Robert's 20th century life bears witness to phenomenal change across the decades. His profession is transformed by industrial revolution into a corporate powerhouse that fells the forests faster than they can regrow. His youth is born of inspiration from the Old West in all it's simplicity and racism, whilst his elder years see the rise of megacities and the outer space orbit of the Earth. Before it even delves any deeper, Train Dreams is brilliant at showing how the world outpaces us all. The entire film consists of the varying meetings and partings we experience through life, stressing how so few of them are within our control. We don't always get to meet people on our terms, and we don't always get the goodbyes that we would like. And whilst Robert's life is full of the unique hardships that come from living off the land, his emotional journey is far more universal. He endures insurmountable grief, he feels like an imposter as both age and the world advance on him, and he goes through all manner of different connections in life that shape his own existence in ways both big and small. Train Dreams remarks that the smallest insect is as vital as the mighty river, but also that everything within the world looks very small when you look at the vastness of it all. The sentiment goes that life has no real innate meaning or purpose, but that that can be okay if we make our peace with it somehow. Beautifully shot, Train Dreams allows the scenery to lift just as heavily as the acting and the writing do. None of it is slight, and yet it always feels like we're at arms length. Robert lives, laughs and loves as much as the next man, but he embodies that age old paradox of feeling like someone we completely relate to whilst also feeling like we really don't know him at all. Joel Edgerton does a superb job portraying Robert - a somewhat introverted man but equally personable and vulnerable, whilst convincing us that he fits in to this challenging post-West scene. An assortment of other faces you'll be trying to identify crop up throughout, each leaving an impression on Robert, but equally on us - as the anecdotal encounters Robert enjoys throughout his life are genuinely engaging. You know when you get that fleeting, bittersweet connection to someone you're going to only know for the shortest of times? This film depicts that sensation brilliantly. The random colleague you work with more than once, the passenger on the train you strike up a conversation with, the man at the local store who's only ever said five words to you and yet you feel you know him. Train Dreams revels in those sorts of encounters - the ones you remember years later. So much of this film is about memory, and the finite lifespan of it. We're shown in several ways how memories are as mortal as the people who possess them, and their fading is a cause for grief as much as the passing of any actual person. Train Dreams lingers in memories, the whole film narrated retrospectively, even. Whilst much of the film dwells in depressing spaces and haunting thoughts, it aims for a lighter conclusion that differs from the source material (which opts for a somewhat more downbeat climax) - this divergence works fine, but might well be the only weak link in a film that otherwise strives to not insult the emotional intelligence of the viewer. Make no mistake, the film is still something of an acquired taste given it moves about as fast as the ancient glaciers it references, but it's mostly a film rooted in feeling, and isn't afraid to prioritise a lingering scene defined by dialogue over a scene where things are physically happening all of the time. Train Dreams is engaging, contemplative, and evocative but never slight. It paints a simple image, through which the most elaborate emotions can be experienced, and the futility of life can be reckoned with - in all it's lack of meaning. -- 89% -- Train Dreams ranked in 2025
